newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court upholds national law restricting debt collection.
newsitem.headline: Court upholds national law restricting debt collection.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Thursday member states may restrict the right to pursue judicial debt collection to lawyers.
A creditor based in Germany pursued a debtor through a French based debt collection agency, INC Consulting SARL (INC).
INC gave power-of-attorney to its managing director, Ramthun, residing in Germany, to enforce the judicial decision obtained in Germany, against the debtor.

When Ramthun sought attachment of the debtor's assets, the application was dismissed on the grounds that she lacked capacity to act, as debt-collection undertakings are prohibited from representing creditor clients.

Although the court found that issues of the right to provide services under article 59 of the EC treaty were at stake in this case, it made allowance for German law which requires debt collection work to be made through the services of a lawyer.

The German law "constitutes a restriction on the freedom to provide services ... albeit it applies without distinction to national providers of services and those of other member states..." the court said.

"As Community law presently stands, it is for the member states to assess whether it it necessary to place restricitons on the professional recovery of debts by way of judicial proceedings," the court said.
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: German)
"Freedom to provide services - Judicial recovery of debts - Authorization - Article 59 of the EC treaty"
Reference from teh Langericht dortmund, Germany for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings between
on the interpretation of the provisions of the EC Treaty relataing to freedom to provide services, in particular article 59

Article 59 of the EC treaty does not preclude a national rule which prohibits an undertaking established in another member state from securing judicial recovery of debs owed to others on business entitiies the ground that the exercise of that activity ina professional capacity is reserved to the legal profession.
